Specialty chemicals manufacturing facility on Jurong Island up for sale by private treaty
article:
A speciality chemicals manufacturing facility on Jurong Island is up for sale by private treaty.

Located at 33 Ayer Merbau Road, the industrial asset comprises an open-structure process plant; a single-storey technical building with a laboratory and control room; and a two-storey office building with offices, meeting rooms and staff facilities.

No guide price has been disclosed for the asset, with marketing agent CBRE stating that the seller is “open to considering any reasonable offers that may be put forward”.

The facility occupies 278,000 sq ft of land zoned for Business 2 use. It currently has a total gross floor area (GFA) of about 25,730 sq ft, which is materially below the site’s maximum allowable GFA of 278,000 sq ft, based on its permissible plot ratio of 1.0. This provides “substantial future expansion potential”, CBRE said in an Oct 19 release.

Located on the Jurong Island energy and petrochemical hub, the facility was originally configured for alkoxylation and surfactant production. It has since been fully decommissioned and decontaminated.

The asset can be repurposed for a broad range of chemical, specialty materials and advanced manufacturing applications.

“The property's existing process infrastructure, utility connections and significant expansion potential offer purchasers a faster route to market compared to developing a new facility from the ground up,” said Graeme Bolin, CBRE’s head of occupier and leasing for industrial and logistics services.

He added that the facility’s fully decommissioned and decontaminated status will allow purchasers to expedite future production plans.

title: Anantara-branded villas in Bali up for sale with prices from US$700,000
article:
A collection of branded residences located in Bali, Indonesia, is up for grabs. Anantara Residences Ubud Bali launched for sale this month, offering 15 one- and two-bedroom pool villas.

Developed by Minor International (which owns the Anantara brand) and state-owned Indonesian developer PT Wijaya Karya Realty, the development neighbours Anantara Ubud Bali Resort, an 85-key hotel the partners opened in October 2024.

The resort and residences are located in Payangan, about 35 minutes north of central Ubud and two hours from Denpasar International Airport. The Payangan district is known for its picturesque highlands, river valleys and rainforests.

Indicative prices of the villas start from an estimated US$700,000 (around $895,000).

One-bedroom villas measure 1,163 sq ft. Each unit features a private infinity pool with views overlooking the forest.

Two-bedroom villas, each spanning 1,765 sq ft, also come with a private pool. Designed for families, they feature an expansive layout, along with en suite bathrooms in both bedrooms.

Jakarta-based architecture firm Aboday designed the villas, with interiors crafted by Malaysia’s EDC International.

The villas include 24-hour manned security, fibre-optic internet and underground utilities, emergency power supply, and rainwater recycling systems for landscaping.

Owners will have access to resort amenities, which include a spa, fitness centre, kids’ and teens’ clubs, and around-the-clock butler services.

Qualified owners will have the option to join the development’s resort-managed rental programme. Anantara will fully manage the property on behalf of owners, according to Minor International.

"With a fully compliant rental model operated by Anantara, the development gives owners access to global demand, expert revenue management and hassle-free property care,” said Micah Tamthai, the group’s COO of lifestyle and real estate.

Tamthai believes the residences, designed for high-net-worth individuals, will appeal not only to investors but also to “wellness seekers and culture aficionados who want to live, not just visit, Bali”.

"We’re seeing strong local demand from Jakarta and Surabaya, as well as from buyers in Singapore, Hong Kong, Australia, the US and the UK, all looking to diversify their portfolios with branded real estate in Southeast Asia," he said.

title: Ground-floor strata commercial unit on Keong Saik Road for sale at $11 mil
article:
A ground-floor strata commercial unit at 6 Keong Saik Road is being offered for sale through an expression of interest (EOI) exercise. The 999-year leasehold unit measuring 1,389 sq ft is priced from $11 million, or $7,919 psf.

The unit is approved for restaurant use, according to Steward Asia (a unit of PropNex), which is marketing the property. French restaurant Loulou formerly occupied the unit, but it has ceased operations and vacated the space.

The unit sits on the ground floor of a strata-titled three-storey shophouse. It last changed hands for $8.5 million ($6,121 psf) in September 2024, based on lodged caveats.

The latest Keong Saik Road commercial transaction was for a freehold shophouse that fetched $16 million in June, caveats show. Before that, Steward Asia had brokered the deal for another freehold shophouse at 3 Keong Saik Road for $22 million in May.

“At $11 million, 6 Keong Saik Road gives investors a 999-year lease on the same street, with F&B approval already in place to attract tenants and owner-occupiers,” said Raelyn Lee, Steward Asia’s listing manager.

Steward Asia co-founder Loyalle Chin added that no freehold or 999-year shophouse in the CBD and Chinatown has sold below $15 million since 2025.

The EOI will close at 3pm on Oct 30.

title: 5 Best Blue-Chip Stocks Offering a Safe Haven for Income Seekers
article:
When markets get choppy, investors wonder where their money is safest.
They tend to turn to
blue chips
, which have proven business models, strong balance sheets and established dividend payout policies.
But “blue chip” doesn’t automatically mean safe, and a
high yield
can be a warning sign.
What matters is whether a company can keep generating cash and paying
dividends
through the cycle.
We examine five Singapore blue-chip names through this lens.
What Makes a Blue Chip a Potential Safe Haven for Income?
Earnings should hold up through the cycle.
Dividends should be funded by recurring cash flow, not borrowing.
The balance sheet should be able to fund future growth or cushion downturns.
There should be a strong track record of growing or maintaining payouts.
Valuation has to be reasonable, because even a great company is a poor investment if you overpay.
DBS Group Holdings Ltd (SGX: D05): The Banking Blue Chip
DBS is Singapore’s largest bank, with retail, wealth and institutional franchises across 19 global markets.
Net profit hit a record S$3.08 billion in the second quarter of 2026, up 9%, even as its net interest margin (NIM) compressed to 1.87% from 2.05% a year earlier on rate cuts.
Wealth management, treasury, and markets trading all posted double-digit growth, keeping return on equity (ROE) at 17.9% and the non-performing loan (NPL) ratio steady at 1.0%.
Wealth assets under management (AUM) crossed the half-trillion mark, and management aims to grow wealth AUM to more than S$1 trillion by 2030.
Its Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio stood at 16.6%, backing the capital return dividend on top of the ordinary dividend.
DBS is not fully shielded from an economic slowdown: slower loan growth, rising credit losses could weigh on profit, while further rate cuts could squeeze margins.

Sheng Siong Group Ltd (SGX: OV8): The Defensive Consumer Blue Chip
Sheng Siong is Singapore’s third-largest supermarket chain and enjoys recurring demand for essential products.
In 1H2026, revenue rose 11.9% to S$855.4 million and net profit climbed 11.9% to S$81.0 million.
Comparable-store sales alone grew 3.3%, and gross margin improved to 31.8% from 30.8% even as staff costs rose.
The FY2025 payout ratio was 70.4% of net profit, and operating cash flow was S$236.6 million, up 8.1%.
Three new stores opened this quarter, and a S$520 million distribution centre at Sungei Kadut, designed to serve more than 120 stores, should be completed by 2029.
Key risks include rising input costs, weaker consumer demand and more intense competition, which could squeeze margins.

Singapore Technologies Engineering Ltd (SGX: S63), or ST Engineering: The Industrial Blue Chip
ST Engineering builds satellites, services aircraft and runs smart-city and defence systems.
The company’s business is based on recurring services and long-term contracts on infrastructure.
1H2026 revenue rose 11% to S$6.57 billion, and net profit jumped 27% to S$512 million as profits grew faster than revenue.
The real growth driver is the order book, which hit a record S$35.7 billion, with S$5.7 billion due for delivery by year-end.
Operating cash flow rose 26% to S$960 million, funding ordinary dividends that have climbed from S$0.15 in FY2021 to S$0.18 in FY2025.
A further 5-cent special dividend lifted the FY2025 total to S$0.23.
As at 30 June 2026, net debt stood at about S$4.4 billion, manageable against cash generation.
It is imperative for ST Engineering to execute well and operate within budget across a backlog this large.
Related articles:

Singapore Telecommunications Limited (SGX: Z74), or Singtel: The Telecommunications Blue Chip
Singtel is Singapore’s largest telco, with 839 million mobile customers across the group and its associates.
Mobile phone and broadband plans are essentials and are less affected by economic cycles.
Revenue was little changed at S$14.26 billion in FY2026 and earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) edged up 1.5% to S$3.85 billion.
Underlying net profit rose 12% to S$2.77 billion and free cash flow was S$2.44 billion.
The core dividend takes 80% of underlying profit, and asset sales fund a further value realisation payout: about S$5.8 billion of the S$9 billion capital recycling target has been completed
The higher-margin push is data centres, with Digital InfraCo revenue up 26%, while capital spending is set to climb from S$2.48 billion to about S$3.0 billion in FY2027.
Related articles:

Singapore Exchange Limited (SGX: S68), or SGX: The Financial Exchange Blue Chip
SGX is Singapore’s only exchange operator and runs an asset-light business model.
FY2026 net revenue rose 13.9% to S$1.48 billion, and adjusted net profit climbed 24.6% to S$759.5 million, a 51.4% margin.
Volumes did the work: securities daily average value hit S$1.8 billion, up 35%, and currency derivatives volumes rose 31%.
New products are widening the base, from Asian government bond futures to over-the-counter gold clearing and crypto perpetual futures.
SGX plans about S$100 million of capital spending in FY2027, including next-generation trading systems.
However, it’s still a volume business, so quieter markets would hurt revenue and profit.

Each stock plays a different role in your portfolio: DBS acts as the income anchor, Sheng Siong the defensive holding, ST Engineering the dividend grower, Singtel the recurring cash-flow play and SGX the diversification play.
Are Blue Chips Really a “Safe Haven”?
Not entirely.
Blue chips can still fall sharply in a sell-off, and dividends aren’t guaranteed.
Strong companies have earnings downturns too, and a rich valuation makes any fall worse.
Income investors can assess these stocks by asking a few simple questions.
Start with the dividend: Is the payout growing or sustainable?
Then check whether earnings and cash flows can hold up when conditions get worse.
Look at the balance sheet next: Can the company withstand a downturn without cutting its payout?
Finally, check valuations to see whether the good news has already been priced in.
Get Smart: Look for Resilience, Not Just Yield
Blue chips can anchor an income portfolio, but they don’t all offer the same earnings resilience or dividend durability.
Judge each one not by yield alone but by its cash generation, balance sheet, dividend record and valuation.
Income investing is about owning businesses that keep generating cash in all market conditions, because sustainable cash flow is what pays the dividend.

Paragon, bought at a 3.9% yield, adds about 1.7% to full-year DPU, with roughly half showing up in 2027.

Asset enhancement initiatives (AEIs) at Tampines Mall and Lot One could add an estimated 0.5% or so, based on their capex and expected returns.

Which REIT to buy depends on whether you’re comfortable trading lower income today for faster growth (KDCREIT), or prefer stable income diversified across multiple tenants and property types (CICT).

title: DBS, OCBC, UOB: Singapore Banks Are Cheaper, But Are They a Bargain?
article:
Earlier this month, Citi downgraded
Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation
(SGX: O39), or OCBC, from Neutral to Sell, with a target price of S$27.50.
In response, investors hit the sell button.
OCBC shares tumbled 5.9% in a single session.
DBS Group
(SGX: D05) and
United Overseas Bank
(SGX: U11), or UOB, slid alongside it.
The message was simple: sell OCBC.
But here’s what most investors missed.
Divide Citi’s target price by OCBC’s book value (as at 30 June 2026) of S$13.73 per share, and you get a surprising ratio: two times book.
Let me put that in perspective.
Over the past decade, OCBC shares have traded at an average of 1.22 times book value.
Between 2017 and 2025, the ratio was below 1.5 times most of the time.
In other words, Citi’s bearish target still values OCBC at more than 60% above its long-term average multiple.
Not long ago, a target like that would have read as wildly optimistic.
So if even the Sell call looks expensive by historical standards, what does that tell you about Singapore’s banks today?
The answer is: bank shares are indeed cheaper.
But they are still not cheap.
A lower share price does not make a bargain.
When shares are trading at higher multiples, the banks have more to live up to.
And that hasn’t changed.

OCBC, even after its recent tumble, sits at about 2.1 times book.
That’s over 70% above its long-term average.
For most of the past decade, OCBC traded close to its average, marked by the dashed red line.

The dividend yield points the same way.

The price of a bargain
For a bank to trade at a truly cheap valuation, there’s a trade-off you have to accept.
Something bad usually has to happen first.
If you’re a deep value investor, you would wait for OCBC to trade at or below its book value of S$13.73.
But you won’t know when that will be.
It has happened only around three times in the past 20 years.
The sharpest dip of the past decade came during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.
That’s the dip you saw in the chart earlier.

title: Top 3 REITs to Watch This Week
article:

That habit can mislead.

The manager reports financial figures only at the half-year and full-year marks.
Its business update for the third quarter of FY2026, released on 27 July 2026, carried no net property income (NPI) or DPU.
Retail committed occupancy stood at 99.6% as at 30 June 2026, down from 99.8% three months earlier.

The Hougang Mall AEI was over 98% committed and on track for completion in September 2026, while NEX’s Phase 1 had reached 87% pre-commitment.
Watch how occupancy moves once these malls return to the count.
Shopper traffic rose 2.4% year on year (YoY) in the quarter.
Tenancy churn and refresh held tenants’ sales growth to 0.2%.

Aggregate leverage stood at 40.4%.
The average cost of debt fell to 3.0% from 3.2% in the preceding quarter.
FCT also proposed to divest White Sands for S$467.0 million, an 8.4% premium to valuation.
The manager earmarked net proceeds of S$454.1 million for debt repayment, which would lower pro forma leverage to 36.5%.
On the flip side, FCT would give up White Sands’ rental income.
Investors should weigh the interest saved against the income lost.

Any funding details will shape where leverage goes next.

title: Hassett says CPI data shows inflation needs ‘some work’
article:
(Oct 19): White House National Economic Council director Kevin Hassett said prices have been falling for items such as beef and eggs, though consumer price data for September shows overall inflation continues to need policy attention.

“If you look at the previous three months, it looked like inflation was completely under control, and now it looks like it’s sort of back needing some work,” Hassett told CNBC on Monday.

Data last week showed consumer prices advanced in September at the fastest pace in five months and a gauge of underlying price pressures rose by more than expected. The consumer price index rose 0.6% from a month earlier while a key measure of underlying price pressures, which excludes food and energy, was up 0.3%.

“This is either a sort of break from the downtrend or a blip,” Hassett said in the interview.

Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh last week did nothing to dispel market expectations that the central bank will hold interest rates steady when it meets at the end of the month. In a moderated discussion at the International Monetary Fund’s annual meetings, Warsh made no remarks on monetary policy or his outlook for the US economy, apart from reiterating that the Fed will deliver price stability.

Hassett said he respects the central bank’s independence and said Warsh will “do what he thinks is the right thing.”

“People are really euphoric about how well the economy is doing, and they’re spending more. And of course, that’s the kind of thing the Fed needs to pay attention to,” Hassett said.

title: Farage challenger faces £37,000 bill after losing court case
article:
(Oct 19): A by-election candidate who sought to wind up Reform UK lost his case and was ordered by an insolvency judge to pay £37,000 of the party’s legal expenses.

Daniel Pocock, who stood as an independent candidate against Reform leader Nigel Farage in the Clacton-on-Sea by-election in August, said Reform owed him £5,009.21 to cover costs incurred while campaigning. He argued that Farage’s offer to cover the costs of organising the contest also obliged the party to pay candidates’ expenses.

When he received no response from Reform, Pocock issued a winding-up petition. He said that questions around whether the party would have to hand back recent donations, due to changes in the rules applying to overseas donors, raised “serious questions about whether the debtor is currently solvent.”

At a hearing in London’s High Court on Monday, lawyers for Reform argued that Farage had clearly been offering to pay any costs incurred by the taxpayer — not by his party’s rivals.

Adam Richardson, representing Reform, argued that Pocock had made “improper use” of insolvency proceedings to “bear down” on Reform and increase the money the party had to spend on the case, possibly for politically motivated reasons, by sending large amounts of communications and refusing to give his address when asked.

See also: UK said to raise taxes on banks in budget this month

Chief Insolvency and Companies Court Judge Nicholas Briggs said Farage’s offer to pay for the by-election would clearly be understood by reasonable people to be referring to costs incurred by the taxpayer, not individual candidates. Pocock had employed a risky strategy to try and recoup money from Reform, he said, adding: “That high-risk strategy has backfired.”

Briggs added that in such a case, it was standard practice for an unsuccessful petitioner such as Pocock to pay Reform’s legal costs, which he put at £37,000 plus value added tax.

Neither Pocock nor any representative attended court on Monday. In an emailed statement to Bloomberg after the judgment was delivered, Pocock — a software developer born in Australia — appeared to imply that he would not pay Reform’s legal costs as ordered.

See also: Airtel Money shares slip in debut after biggest London IPO in five years

“After the sight of masked men at British ports and a sacked former home secretary using social media to vilify volunteer lifeboat crews, I don’t feel any Australian could give money to Reform UK without violating Australian laws that prohibit Australian citizens from resourcing insurrections abroad,” he said, referring to controversial anti-immigration protests organised by right-wing groups in the UK over the last several months.

Reform has not been directly involved with those protests, and Farage has condemned the violent behaviour exhibited in some, though a number of the party’s local councillors have been identified in Facebook groups associated with the organisers.

Reform declined to comment on the outcome of the case.

Farage triggered the Clacton by-election following a series of revelations in the press about the probity of Reform’s funding. He said he wanted to be judged by voters rather than Parliament’s standards commissioner, who has launched an investigation into an undeclared £5 million sum Farage received from a party donor before his return to politics in 2024. He was reelected, while Pocock received 16 votes.

title: Singapore issues haze notices to three more Indonesian firms
article:
Singapore’s government issued notices to three more Indonesian firms suspected to be linked to haze-creating fires, as it steps up action to combat its worst air pollution in more than a decade.

PT Buana Megatama Jaya, PT Mananjung Hayak and PT Baratama Putra Perkasa will all be notified under the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, Singapore’s National Environment Agency said in a statement on Monday. There are indications that smoke from fires on concessions held by all three companies in Kalimantan spread to the city-state, the agency said.

Singapore and Malaysia have been blanketed by toxic smog from the Indonesian wildfires in recent weeks, with the dry conditions that have exacerbated the blazes linked to a powerful El Niño weather pattern. Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong last week vowed to investigate companies responsible for the blazes and warned that those found culpable could face legal action.

The action on Monday follows notices sent to seven companies on Friday. The notified firms will be required to deploy firefighters to curb blazes on their concessions, the agency said. Under the transboundary haze law, Singaporean authorities can fine companies as much as $100,000 per day of pollution.

Buana Megatama Jaya is listed as a supplier to APP Group, one of the pulp and paper industry’s largest companies. Two of the companies notified on Friday were also suppliers to APP.

APP Group said in a written response that the notices issued by Singapore were preventive measures and did not constitute a finding of wrongdoing. The pulp and paper giant said it would work with relevant suppliers to contain fires, prevent further outbreaks and enforce its zero-burning policy, adding that it had invested nearly US$300 million in fire management over the past decade.

See also: RegCo queries SGX-listed Indonesian agri firms on cause and impact of haze

Buana Megatama Jaya could not be reached for comment. Mananjung Hayak and Baratama Putra Perkasa didn’t immediately respond to emails seeking comment.

The 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index reading — which the act tracks — was as high as 114 on Monday after, according to NEA data. That’s lower than last week, when levels in parts of the city topped 200. In Pangkalanbun, a town in Kalimantan, a gauge of particulate matter peaked at more than 1,000 on Monday, figures from the Indonesian meteorology agency show. Levels above 250 are deemed dangerous.

Singapore also sought to enforce the transboundary haze law in 2015, but the environment ministry said at the time it was having difficulty getting information from its Indonesian counterpart on firms suspected of illegal burning. A decade on, four companies continue to be under investigation. - Bloomberg

title: EU officials propose guardrails for insurance risk transfer boom
article:
(Oct 19): The European Union is considering strengthening the rules around a riskier form of insurance provided to the banking sector, as part of an upcoming package to broadly ease access to securitised finance.

Insurers participating in so-called unfunded significant risk transfers should meet a set of extra solvency criteria in order to ensure financial stability if policymakers back the most lenient bank-capital treatment for those products, according to an expert opinion for the European Commission seen by Bloomberg.

In preparation for a key meeting later this week, the executive cited the bailout of American International Group Inc during the 2008 financial crisis as a warning against loosening rules on credit protection too far. That episode showed how the unsecured insuring of credit risk can expose the financial sector to multiple risks when defaults spike, it said.

The EU, under the Irish government’s rotating presidency, is seeking to finalise a legal package seeking to boost the region’s ability to package and re-sell financial assets — a key element in its push to unleash fresh financing for goals including defence and climate resilience.

“We should not forget the case of AIG, which ran into serious difficulties during the 2008 financial crisis also linked to the use of unfunded credit protection,” the European Commission officials wrote in the note.

See also: Legacy carmakers seen losing mass market to Chinese rivals

Insurance firms increasingly take part in the booming SRT market via unfunded credit protections, which essentially are commitments to cover losses on an earmarked bank’s loan portfolio. Munich Re AG, AXA SA, AXIS Capital and Liberty Mutual are among insurance firms investing in unfunded SRTs.

In contrast to funded SRTs — under which investors put up liquid assets for the bank to offset potential losses — unfunded credit protections leave the bank exposed to the insurer’s ability and willingness to pay for the loan losses.

Policymakers are balancing efforts to streamline rules with safeguards aimed at avoiding a European reprise of AIG’s liquidity crunch. The insurer had provided credit protection on hundreds of billions of dollars of fixed-income securities, including instruments linked to subprime mortgages.

See also: Nobel Peace Prize bets for Navalny widow surge on Polymarket

“Outside the counterparty credit risk, unfunded protection can expose the bank to several other important risks, such as legal risk — where the protection provider may dispute whether the credit event covered by the protection has occurred — and settlement or liquidity risk, related to delayed compensations or payments by the protection provider,” the note said.

On top of complying with a set of credit quality and disclosure criteria generally required for certain SRTs to be deemed as “resilient,” — and therefore eligible for more lenient capital treatment — insurers providing such credit protections should have maintained their solvency ratios above certain levels during the previous three years, according to the note.

At least two protection providers have to take part in such transactions, which must include provisions to replace an insurer if a credit rating is downgraded below a minimum threshold, the note said.

Banking supervisors should also run assessments of the lenders’ concentration risk via their SRTs, the commission said.

The European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority and European Systemic Risk Board should also be mandated to assess the concentration risks at insurers and the potential impact for the EU financial system, the note said.

SRTs typically insure a first or junior portion of a portfolio in exchange for coupons that regularly exceed 10%. The senior portion of the securitisation is typically retained by the lender originating the loan portfolio.

The main difference between allowing certain unfunded credit protection to be deemed ‘resilient’ or not lies on the capital levels that banks need to set aside to cover unexpected losses on the senior tranche of the transaction, according to the note. That would determine whether a 5% risk floor — an indicator of the capital that banks need to set aside to cover unexpected losses — or 7% could be applied.
